title: Empirical Properties of Correlation

maps.tested: Both sheets reduce the chapter to two items.
maps.specifics: Named: 'identifying best-fit distribution (equity, bond and default correlation)' and 'know calculation of mean reversion and autocorrelation.' Which distribution best fits which correlation type is a three-way sibling swap; the mean-reversion rate is obtained by regressing the correlation change on the lagged level.

vardeezReading: MR-9: Moderate; his note names two things, identifying the best-fit distribution (equity, bond and default correlation) and knowing the calculation of mean reversion and the autocorrelation concept.

los.vardeez: Mean reversion calculation and autocorrelation concept
Best-fit distribution for equity, bond and default correlation

selectors.name: Best-fit distribution by correlation type
selectors.what: Which distribution best fits equity, bond and default probability correlations: Johnson SB for equity and for default probability correlations, generalised extreme value for bond correlations (the normal also fits bond correlations quite well). Normal, lognormal and beta fit equity correlations poorly, and the state of the economy changes the equity fit only slightly and not significantly.

selectors.name: Mean reversion rate from regression
selectors.what: Regress the correlation change S(t) - S(t-1) on the lagged level S(t-1): the slope is -a, so the mean reversion rate a is the absolute value of the slope, and the intercept is a x mu, so the long-term mean is intercept / a. Also the one-step forecast S(t) = S(t-1) + a x (mu - S(t-1)).
selectors.theory: Mean reversion is the pull of a variable back to its long-term mean and is present when the change is negatively related to the lagged level; in the discrete Vasicek form 0 <= a <= 1, with a = 1 a full pull back each step, a = 0.5 halfway and a = 0 none. A forecast that uses the slope with its sign pushes the correlation away from the mean.

selectors.name: Autocorrelation from mean reversion rate
selectors.what: The one-lag autocorrelation corresponding to a mean reversion rate: AC = cov(rho(t), rho(t-1)) / (sigma(rho(t)) x sigma(rho(t-1))), which in the study is approximately 1 - a (mean reversion 79.03% gives autocorrelation 20.97%).
selectors.theory: Autocorrelation is the degree to which a variable is correlated with its past values, algebraically the Pearson coefficient; it is the opposite property of mean reversion, so strong mean reversion means low autocorrelation, and positive autocorrelation is called persistence.
